summary: Records the IETF consensus that no update was needed to the IDNA character rules in RFC 5892 when Unicode 6.0 came out. Only three code points from Unicode 5.2 had changed property values, and the rules still held.

plainLanguage.summary: Domain names can use letters from many languages, and the allowed-letter list depends on Unicode. A new Unicode version came out, and this note says nothing needed to change.

subtitle: Unicode 6.0 changes do not require IDNA rule updates.

tldr.problem: Unicode 6.0 changed the character category of three code points that had been assigned in Unicode 5.2, potentially affecting which characters are valid in internationalized domain names under RFC 5892.
tldr.mechanism: Analyze the three changed code points (Kannada characters and New Tai Lue digit) against the IDNA rules to determine if updates are necessary.
tldr.outcome: IETF consensus is that no changes to RFC 5892 are required; the three characters are unlikely to appear in actual domain names anyway.

today: RFC 6452 is a Standards Track document and an informational clarification of IDNA policy. RFC 5892 remains the current IDNA specification without modification due to Unicode 6.0.

sections.title: When Unicode changes matter
sections.content: Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA), defined in RFC 5892, uses Unicode character properties to determine which characters are allowed in domain names. IDNA was defined when Unicode 5.0 was current (later updated to 5.2). When Unicode 6.0 was released, three code points had their character category changed: two Kannada signs changed from Symbol-Other to Letter-Other, and one New Tai Lue digit changed from Number-Decimal to Number-Other. These changes could theoretically affect which characters pass IDNA validation.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for what letters you can use in domain names depend on what Unicode says those letters are. Unicode got updated and changed what three symbols are classified as.

sections.title: The three changed characters
sections.content: U+0CF1 (Kannada Sign Jihvamuliya) changed from Symbol-Other to Letter-Other, making it PVALID instead of DISALLOWED. U+0CF2 (Kannada Sign Upadhmaniya) also changed from Symbol-Other to Letter-Other, making it PVALID instead of DISALLOWED. U+19DA (New Tai Lue Tham Digit One) changed from Number-Decimal to Number-Other, making it DISALLOWED instead of PVALID. These changes represent non-backward-compatible modifications to the IDNA derived property values.
sections.plainLanguage: Two Indian letter marks became more allowed, and one Thai digit became less allowed. The opposite changes to each other.

sections.title: IETF consensus and impact
sections.content: The IETF consensus, reflected in RFC 6452, is that no change to RFC 5892 is required based on Unicode 6.0 changes. The three code points are unlikely to occur in internationalized domain names in practice, so the security implications are minor. This consensus does not imply that future Unicode updates will not require RFC 5892 changes. RFC 6452 was produced because Unicode 6.0 was the first version released after IDNA2008 was published, establishing the precedent for how IETF will handle future Unicode versions.
sections.plainLanguage: These three characters are so rare in domain names that the change doesn't matter. But this document shows how IETF will handle future Unicode updates.
